apparatus.purpose: Massive cast-iron bench vise with vulcanized leather clamp jaws designed to firmly grip the rod at its exact nodal center without damping longitudinal vibrations.

apparatus.name: Lycopodium Powder / Fine Cork Dust
apparatus.purpose: Dehydrated, uniform microscopic spores (clubmoss) providing high fluidic mobility to form sharp, well-defined nodal heap striations under acoustic excitation.

apparatus.name: Excitation Cloth and Rosin
apparatus.purpose: Coarse woolen or leather cloth impregnated with powdered rosin to stroke the free half of the metal rod and excite strong longitudinal vibrations.

procedure.title: Apparatus Inspection and Powder Distribution
procedure.text: Thoroughly dry the interior of the Kundt's glass tube using a dry flannel swab. Distribute a light, uniform track of dry lycopodium powder or fine cork dust along the entire bottom length of the horizontal tube by gently rocking and tapping the tube cradle.
procedure.why: Moisture causes the powder to clump and adhere to the glass walls, destroying the delicate aerodynamic sensitivity needed to resolve acoustic node boundaries.

procedure.title: Rod Centering and Midpoint Clamping
procedure.text: Measure the total length of the brass rod L_rod with a steel meter rule. Mark the exact geometric center (L_rod / 2) with a fine pencil line, and clamp the rod firmly in the heavy vise jaws at this exact midpoint, ensuring the cork disc enters the tube mouth without touching the glass walls.
procedure.why: The fundamental longitudinal mode requires a displacement node at the exact center; clamping off-center damps the fundamental oscillation and excites dissonant higher overtones.

procedure.title: Piston Alignment and Tube Coupling
procedure.text: Insert the adjustable reflector piston into the far end of the glass tube. Position the tube so that the vibrating cork disc on the rod penetrates approximately 1 to 2 cm into the near end, ensuring an airtight but frictionless acoustic coupling.
procedure.why: Direct mechanical rubbing between the cork disc and glass wall dissipates acoustic energy, produces severe damping, and risks glass fracture.

procedure.title: Longitudinal Excitation and Standing Wave Tuning
procedure.text: Grip the free protruding end of the brass rod with the rosin-dusted leather cloth. Pull firmly along the axis of the rod toward the free tip with a steady, decisive stroke to emit a piercing, clear musical note. Simultaneously adjust the position of the far reflector piston until the powder inside the tube violently agitates and settles into sharp, well-defined transverse striations.
procedure.why: Standing waves only form when the air column length matches an integral number of acoustic half-wavelengths, establishing constructive interference and maximum acoustic pressure amplitude.

procedure.title: Nodal Spacing Measurement and Averaging
procedure.text: Using the tube's graduated metric scale, record the exact positions of five consecutive well-defined dust heaps (displacement nodes). Calculate the distance between successive heaps and compute the mean nodal spacing d = λ_air / 2.
procedure.why: Measuring across multiple consecutive heaps averages out local powder drift and visual apex reading errors, yielding high precision in wavelength determination.

procedure.title: Length Variation and Systematic Data Acquisition
procedure.text: Repeat the excitation, piston tuning, and nodal distance recording for six distinct calibrated rod lengths (80.0, 90.0, 100.0, 110.0, 120.0, and 130.0 cm). Tabulate rod length L_rod against dust node spacing d for subsequent linear regression.
procedure.why: Systematically varying rod length provides the necessary data range to perform linear regression, isolating the sound velocity ratio v_air / v_rod from any zero-offset artifacts.

topics.title: Acoustic Wave Interference and Longitudinal Standing Waves
topics.text: When two identical longitudinal acoustic waves propagate in opposite directions within a confined tube, their linear superposition produces an acoustic standing wave. Let the two counter-propagating acoustic pressure perturbations be represented by p₁(x, t) = P₀ sin(kx − ωt) and p₂(x, t) = P₀ sin(kx + ωt). Applying trigonometric product-to-sum identities, the resultant acoustic pressure field is p(x, t) = p₁ + p₂ = 2 P₀ sin(kx) cos(ωt). Simultaneously, the acoustic particle displacement ξ(x, t) follows the spatial gradient of pressure: ξ(x, t) = 2 ξ₀ cos(kx) sin(ωt), where ξ₀ = P₀ / (ρ₀ v ω). Crucially, acoustic displacement and acoustic pressure are in space-time quadrature (a quarter-wave spatial phase shift of π/2 radians). At locations where kx = nπ (x = n λ/2), the displacement amplitude reaches a maximum (2 ξ₀), defining displacement antinodes where particle velocity u = ∂ξ/∂t swings violently. At these same positions, sin(kx) = 0, meaning acoustic pressure variations vanish (pressure nodes). Conversely, where kx = (2n + 1)π/2 (x = (2n + 1) λ/4), particle displacement is strictly zero (displacement nodes), while acoustic pressure fluctuations reach their peak amplitude (2 P₀, pressure antinodes). At the rigid reflector piston, the solid boundary enforces zero particle displacement (u = 0, displacement node) and complete acoustic reflection with zero phase shift in pressure.
topics.formula: p(x, t) = 2 P_0 \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t), \qquad \xi(x, t) = 2 \xi_0 \cos(kx) \sin(\omega t), \qquad u = \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial t}
topics.question: In a Kundt's tube, do the dust heaps form at displacement nodes or displacement antinodes, and why?
topics.answer: Dust heaps accumulate at displacement nodes. At displacement nodes, acoustic particle velocity is zero, so dust particles remain undisturbed and settle quietly. In contrast, at displacement antinodes, acoustic particle velocity is maximal, generating violent air agitation and radiation pressure that sweep the dust away into striations.

topics.title: Longitudinal Elastic Vibrations in Clamped Solid Rods
topics.text: Longitudinal wave propagation through a solid elastic rod of uniform cross-section A, density ρ, and Young's modulus E is governed by the 1D wave equation: ∂²u/∂t² = v_rod² (∂²u/∂x²), where the phase velocity is given by v_rod = √(E / ρ). In Kundt's experiment, the rod is clamped rigidly at its exact midpoint (x = 0), leaving both ends (x = −L_rod/2 and x = +L_rod/2) entirely free. The rigid clamp enforces a zero-displacement boundary condition at the center: u(0, t) = 0 (displacement node). At the free ends, the longitudinal mechanical stress must vanish: σ = E (∂u/∂x) = 0, which requires the spatial derivative to vanish, creating displacement antinodes (strain nodes). The spatial mode function for anti-symmetric displacement is u_n(x) = C sin(k_n x). Enforcing the free-end condition cos(k_n L_rod / 2) = 0 yields k_n L_rod / 2 = (2n − 1) π / 2, or k_n = (2n − 1) π / L_rod for n = 1, 2, 3, ... For the fundamental longitudinal mode (n = 1), k₁ = π / L_rod, which corresponds to an acoustic wavelength of λ_rod = 2π / k₁ = 2 L_rod. Thus, the rod vibrates in half-wave resonance with its fundamental natural frequency given by f₁ = v_rod / λ_rod = v_rod / (2 L_rod). Clamping exactly at the center suppresses all even harmonics and supports only odd harmonic overtones f_n = (2n − 1) f₁.
topics.formula: v_{\text{rod}} = \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{rod}} = 2 L_{\text{rod}}, \qquad f_1 = \frac{v_{\text{rod}}}{2 L_{\text{rod}}} = \frac{1}{2 L_{\text{rod}}} \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}}
topics.question: Why must the metal rod in Kundt's tube be clamped at its exact center rather than at one-quarter of its length to produce the fundamental tone?
topics.answer: The fundamental longitudinal standing wave in a free-free bar has a single displacement node at the exact midpoint (x = L/2) and displacement antinodes at both free ends (λ = 2L). Clamping at the exact midpoint enforces this displacement node without damping the fundamental mode. Clamping at L/4 would suppress the fundamental and force higher harmonic modes.

topics.title: Kundt's Tube Acoustic Coupling and Powder Striation Dynamics
topics.text: The operational brilliance of Kundt's tube lies in using a lightweight indicator powder to visualize microscopic acoustic wave motion. A small, light cork or cardboard disc mounted on the free end of the vibrating rod projects into the glass tube mouth, acting as an acoustic piston that oscillates back and forth at frequency f. When the air column length is tuned to resonance, stationary standing waves are established with acoustic particle velocity u(x, t) = u_max sin(kx) sin(ωt). The aerodynamic behavior of the fine lycopodium powder or cork dust is governed by acoustic radiation pressure, Bernoulli forces, and Rayleigh acoustic streaming. At displacement antinodes (sin(kx) = ±1), particle velocity oscillates with large amplitudes (often exceeding 1 to 2 m/s). This high velocity creates intense localized aerodynamic drag and Bernoulli suction, which violently lifts the powder off the tube floor and forms characteristic transverse striations (fine parallel ridges perpendicular to the tube axis). At displacement nodes (sin(kx) = 0), the air is completely quiescent: no acoustic forces act on the dust particles, allowing them to remain at rest and accumulate into well-defined, sharp heaps. The spatial distance between any two consecutive heaps corresponds to the distance between adjacent displacement nodes, which is exactly half of the acoustic wavelength in the air: d = λ_air / 2.
topics.formula: d = \frac{\lambda_{\text{air}}}{2} \iff \lambda_{\text{air}} = 2 d, \qquad u_0 = \omega \xi_0 = \frac{P_0}{\rho_0 v_{\text{air}}}
topics.question: How is the distance between two consecutive dust heaps related to the wavelength of sound in air?
topics.answer: The distance between consecutive dust heaps equals half of the acoustic wavelength in air: d = λ_air / 2. Therefore, the full wavelength of sound in air is twice the heap spacing: λ_air = 2d.

topics.title: Comparative Velocity Ratio and Invariant Frequency Equivalence
topics.text: Because the vibrating rod acts as the acoustic driver for the air column, the frequency of the sound waves propagating through the air inside the tube is strictly identical to the mechanical vibration frequency of the rod: f_air = f_rod. Using the universal wave relationship v = f λ for both media, we have: f_air = v_air / λ_air and f_rod = v_rod / λ_rod. Equating these two expressions yields: v_air / λ_air = v_rod / λ_rod. Substituting the fundamental standing wave conditions λ_rod = 2 L_rod and λ_air = 2 d gives: v_air / (2 d) = v_rod / (2 L_rod), which simplifies directly to the classical Kundt velocity relation: v_rod / v_air = L_rod / d. Rearranging for the dust node spacing d yields: d = (v_air / v_rod) L_rod. This powerful relationship demonstrates that the ratio of sound velocities in the solid rod and the gaseous medium equals the ratio of the sounding rod length to the nodal dust spacing. If the speed of sound in air v_air is known from Laplace's adiabatic formula v_air = √(γ R T / M) (v_air = 331.3 √(1 + t / 273.15) m/s, yielding 343.20 m/s at 20.0 °C), the sound velocity in the metal rod can be determined with remarkable accuracy without requiring an electronic frequency counter.
topics.formula: \frac{v_{\text{rod}}}{v_{\text{air}}} = \frac{\lambda_{\text{rod}}}{\lambda_{\text{air}}} = \frac{L_{\text{rod}}}{d} \implies d = \left(\frac{v_{\text{air}}}{v_{\text{rod}}}\right) L_{\text{rod}}, \qquad v_{\text{rod}} = v_{\text{air}} \left(\frac{L_{\text{rod}}}{d}\right)
topics.question: If a brass rod of length 100 cm clamped at its center produces dust heaps spaced 9.81 cm apart in air where sound speed is 343.2 m/s, what is the speed of sound in the rod?

topics.title: Determination of Dynamic Young's Modulus and Continuum Elasticity
topics.text: Kundt's tube provides an elegant method to measure the dynamic Young's modulus E of metals and alloys. From continuum mechanics, the phase velocity of longitudinal waves in an elastic rod whose lateral dimensions are small compared to the wavelength (r << λ) is given by v_rod = √(E / ρ_rod), where ρ_rod is the mass density. Squaring both sides yields: E = ρ_rod v_rod². Combining this with the Kundt velocity ratio gives: E = ρ_rod [v_air (L_rod / d)]². Measuring elastic moduli acoustically offers substantial advantages over static tensile testing (such as hanging weights from a wire). Static tensile tests are vulnerable to mechanical creep, microscopic plastic deformation, thermal expansion drifts, and support compliance. In contrast, acoustic vibrations operate at high audio frequencies (1 kHz to 5 kHz) under infinitesimal strain amplitudes (< 10⁻⁵) and purely adiabatic conditions, measuring the true reversible intermolecular bond stiffness of the crystal lattice. For cold-rolled cartridge brass with density ρ = 8500 kg/m³ and measured wave velocity v_rod = 3500 m/s, the dynamic Young's modulus is E = 8500 × (3500)² = 1.041 × 10¹¹ Pa = 104.1 GPa, in excellent agreement with standard ultrasonic pulse-echo benchmarks.
topics.formula: E = \rho_{\text{rod}} v_{\text{rod}}^2 = \rho_{\text{rod}} \left[ v_{\text{air}} \left(\frac{L_{\text{rod}}}{d}\right) \right]^2, \qquad \sigma_{xx} = E \varepsilon_{xx}
topics.question: How can the dynamic Young's modulus of the brass rod be calculated from the measured speed of sound in the rod?
topics.answer: From the continuum wave equation in a thin elastic bar, v_rod = √(E / ρ_rod). Squaring both sides yields E = ρ_rod v_rod². Given brass density ρ ≈ 8500 kg/m³ and v_rod ≈ 3500 m/s, E ≈ 8500 × 3500² ≈ 1.04 × 10¹¹ Pa = 104 GPa.

topics.title: Linear Regression Formulation and OLS Parameter Isolation
topics.text: To determine the longitudinal wave velocity and Young's modulus with rigorous metrological precision, experimentalists vary the sounding rod length L_rod across a calibrated series (e.g. 80.0 to 130.0 cm) and measure the corresponding mean dust node spacing d. From the theoretical relation d = (v_air / v_rod) L_rod, defining x = L_rod (in metres) as the independent variable and y = d (in metres) as the dependent variable yields the standard linear regression model: y = m x + b. Here, the regression slope m represents the dimensionless acoustic velocity ratio: m = v_air / v_rod. Inverting this relation isolates the longitudinal sound speed in the rod directly: v_rod = v_air / m. The intercept b provides a crucial experimental diagnostic: theoretically b = 0, so any statistically significant non-zero intercept detects end-coupling disc offsets, finite clamp width artifacts, or progressive visual reading bias. Ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression minimizes the sum of squared residuals, averaging out random errors in identifying dust heap crests and yielding unbiased slope and standard error estimates.
topics.formula: d = m L_{\text{rod}} + b \implies m = \frac{v_{\text{air}}}{v_{\text{rod}}} \iff v_{\text{rod}} = \frac{v_{\text{air}}}{m}, \qquad \delta v_{\text{rod}} = v_{\text{air}} \frac{\delta m}{m^2}
topics.question: When plotting dust node spacing d on the vertical axis against rod length L_rod on the horizontal axis, what does the slope m represent?
topics.answer: The slope m = d / L_rod represents the velocity ratio v_air / v_rod. Dividing the known speed of sound in air v_air by the regression slope m directly gives the speed of sound in the metal rod: v_rod = v_air / m.

topics.title: Gas Thermometry, Ratio of Specific Heats (γ), and Modern Applications
topics.text: In addition to investigating solids, Kundt's tube is a classic apparatus for studying the thermodynamics of gases. By sealing the tube and flushing it with test gases (such as Helium, Argon, or Carbon Dioxide), the ratio of specific heats γ = C_p / C_v can be determined. According to Laplace's equation, sound velocity in an ideal gas is v_gas = √(γ R T / M), where R is the universal gas constant, T is absolute temperature, and M is molar mass. Combining this with Kundt's formula gives: d_gas = (v_gas / v_rod) L_rod = (√(γ R T / M) / v_rod) L_rod. Comparing the nodal spacing d_gas in a test gas to d_air in air under identical rod excitation isolates the gas sound velocity: v_gas = v_air (d_gas / d_air). From v_gas, the heat capacity ratio is calculated as γ = (M v_gas²) / (R T). This enabled historical physicists to prove that noble gases like Argon and Helium are monatomic (γ ≈ 1.67, 3 translational degrees of freedom), while air is diatomic (γ ≈ 1.40, 5 degrees of freedom). In modern technology, the standing wave principles of Kundt's tube underpin acoustic levitation of pharmaceutical micro-droplets in containerless processing, thermoacoustic heat pumps and cryo-coolers, and ultrasonic non-destructive testing of structural pipelines.
topics.formula: v_{\text{gas}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}} \implies \gamma = \frac{M v_{\text{gas}}^2}{R T}, \qquad \frac{d_{\text{gas}}}{d_{\text{air}}} = \frac{v_{\text{gas}}}{v_{\text{air}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma_{\text{gas}} M_{\text{air}}}{\gamma_{\text{air}} M_{\text{gas}}}}
topics.question: If the air in Kundt's tube is replaced by carbon dioxide (CO₂, sound speed ≈ 267 m/s) while exciting the same rod, how does the spacing between dust heaps change?
topics.answer: Since d = (v_gas / v_rod) L_rod, the node spacing is directly proportional to the gas sound speed. Because sound travels slower in dense CO₂ (267 m/s) than in air (343.2 m/s), the wavelength is shorter and the dust heaps become closer together by a factor of 267 / 343.2 ≈ 0.78 (7.65 cm instead of 9.81 cm).

quiz.question: In Kundt's tube, the cork dust or lycopodium powder collects into distinct stationary heaps at the:
options: Displacement nodes (points of zero acoustic particle velocity)
Displacement antinodes (points of maximum acoustic particle velocity)
Pressure nodes (points of atmospheric equilibrium pressure)
Positions where acoustic intensity is maximal
quiz.explanation: Dust particles are violently agitated and dispersed at displacement antinodes where acoustic air velocity is greatest. They come to rest and accumulate at displacement nodes where particle motion is zero.

quiz.question: A solid metal rod of length L clamped at its exact center vibrates in its fundamental longitudinal mode. Its acoustic wavelength λ_rod inside the rod is equal to:
options: 2 L
L
4 L
quiz.explanation: Clamping at the midpoint creates a displacement node at the center and displacement antinodes at both free ends. The distance between two adjacent antinodes with a single node between them is one half-wavelength: L = λ / 2, which gives λ = 2 L.

quiz.question: If the distance between consecutive dust heaps in air is measured to be 10.0 cm when driven by a rod vibrating at 1716 Hz, what is the speed of sound in the air inside the tube?
quiz.explanation: The dust heap spacing d = λ_air / 2 = 0.100 m, so λ_air = 0.200 m. Sound velocity is v = f λ = 1716 Hz × 0.200 m = 343.2 m/s.

quiz.question: When plotting dust node spacing d against rod length L_rod, the regression slope is found to be m = 0.0981. If the speed of sound in air is 343.2 m/s, the longitudinal wave speed in the rod is:
quiz.explanation: From d = (v_air / v_rod) L_rod, the slope is m = v_air / v_rod. Therefore, v_rod = v_air / m = 343.2 / 0.0981 ≈ 3498.5 ≈ 3500 m/s.

precautions: Ensure the vibrating cork coupling disc never touches the inner wall of the glass tube during excitation to avoid damping the vibrations or cracking the glass.
Stroke the metal rod strictly in the longitudinal axial direction; avoid lateral or twisting forces that excite undesirable flexural or torsional vibration modes.
Keep the interior of the glass tube completely dry and free of condensation; even slight humidity causes lycopodium powder to aggregate into immobile clusters.
Wear acoustic ear defenders during longitudinal rod excitation, as high-frequency acoustic standing waves can exceed 95 dB SPL near the apparatus.
limitations: The analytical model treats the sounding rod as an ideal, infinitely thin elastic bar with strictly one-dimensional longitudinal stress (Pochhammer-Chree radial inertia dispersion neglected), assumes perfectly planar acoustic wavefronts inside the glass tube with zero viscous tube boundary-layer drag (Helmholtz-Kirchhoff wall attenuation), and models the cork disc as a massless acoustic source. In a physical laboratory, small radial Poisson expansion in thick rods slightly alters overtone frequencies, narrow glass bore introduces small acoustic velocity depression (~0.2% to 0.4% from wall friction), and room temperature gradients cause minor sound velocity shifts in air.

title: Electrostatics: Coulomb's Law, Electric Induction, and Charge Quantification
subject: physics
aim: To investigate electrostatic charge production by friction and induction, verify Faraday's ice-pail experiment and charge conservation, measure the electrostatic force between charged spheres as a function of distance using a Coulomb torsion balance, confirm the inverse-square law, and determine Coulomb's constant and the permittivity of free space using linear regression.
intro: Electrostatics constitutes the cornerstone of classical electromagnetism, describing the fundamental forces, fields, and potentials produced by stationary electric charges. First quantified systematically by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785 using his delicate torsion balance, the electrostatic force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r in vacuum obeys the fundamental inverse-square relationship: F = (1 / 4πε₀) (q₁ q₂ / r²) = k_e (q₁ q₂ / r²), where k_e = 1 / (4πε₀) ≈ 8.98755 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² is Coulomb's constant and ε₀ ≈ 8.85419 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ is the permittivity of free space. Like Newton's law of universal gravitation, Coulomb's law exhibits an inverse-square dependence on distance governed by the geometry of three-dimensional Euclidean space, as formalized by Gauss's flux theorem: ∮ E · dA = Q_enc / ε₀. However, unlike gravity, electrostatic forces are bipolar: charges of like sign repel each other, while charges of opposite sign attract. When two small, identical conducting spheres are charged to equal potentials and placed within a draft-free chamber, the repulsive electrostatic force F deflects a suspended balance beam. By rotating a calibrated torsion head to restore the beam to its initial null position, the applied restoring torque τ = κ θ directly balances the electrostatic torque F · b, yielding an absolute force measurement in the micronewton (μN) regime. Simultaneously, the electrostatic behavior of conductors is governed by Gauss's law: in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field within the bulk of a conductor is identically zero (E = 0), and all excess charge resides exclusively on the outer surface, as demonstrated by Michael Faraday's historic 1843 ice-pail experiment. Furthermore, the surface charge density σ concentrates at regions of high surface curvature (σ ∝ 1/R), generating intense localized electric fields capable of ionizing ambient air into a luminous corona discharge. By recording the electrostatic force F across various separation distances r, ordinary least-squares regression of F against the geometric variable 1/r² yields a strictly linear plot with slope m = k_e q₁ q₂. From this slope and the known sphere charges, students determine Coulomb's constant k_e and the permittivity of free space ε₀ with remarkable precision, bridging classical electrostatic induction, Faraday shielding, and continuum field theory.
fitEquation: F = k_e q_1 q_2 \left(\frac{1}{r^2}\right) \iff y = m x + b \iff k_e = \frac{m}{q^2}, \quad \varepsilon_0 = \frac{1}{4\pi k_e}
settings: Ambient room temperature: T = 20.0 °C; Relative humidity: RH < 25% (Controlled desiccated chamber).
Reference Coulomb electrostatic constant: k_e = 8.98755 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² (Permittivity ε₀ = 8.85419 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹).
Conducting spheres: Precision gold-plated brass (radius a = 5.00 mm, mass m_sphere = 0.445 g).
Sphere electrostatic charge: q₁ = q₂ = 20.00 nC (Regulated contact charging at 3.00 kV DC).
Torsion balance suspension: Phosphor bronze fiber (torsional constant κ = 1.450 × 10⁻⁸ N m rad⁻¹, lever arm b = 10.0 cm).
Chamber boundary: Grounded copper wire Faraday mesh shielding (external stray field attenuation > 99.8%).

apparatus.name: Coulomb Torsion Balance
apparatus.purpose: Precision electrostatic torsion balance housed in a draft-free cylindrical glass chamber with circular degree vernier scale, grounded conductive floor, and low-torsion phosphor bronze suspension fiber.

apparatus.name: Matched Conducting Spheres
apparatus.purpose: Pair of precision-turned, lightweight gold-plated conducting spheres (radius a = 5.0 mm), one suspended on an insulating dielectric balance arm and the other mounted on a graduated sliding carrier.

apparatus.name: Regulated High-Voltage DC Source
apparatus.purpose: Continuously variable low-current power supply (0 to 6.0 kV DC, 50 μA current-limited) for depositing calibrated electrostatic charges on the conducting spheres.

apparatus.name: Precision Proof Plane and Faraday Ice Pail
apparatus.purpose: Polished metallic proof plane disc with amber insulating handle and an insulated nickel-plated Faraday ice pail connected to a digital electrometer for quantitative charge sampling.

apparatus.name: Gold-Leaf Electroscope
apparatus.purpose: Enclosed glass-windowed electroscope with grounded metal shielding case, calibrated leaf divergence protractor, and high-insulation sulfur bushing.

apparatus.name: Desiccated Environmental Chamber
apparatus.purpose: Hermetically sealed chamber enclosure with rechargeable silica gel desiccant column to maintain relative humidity below 25%, preventing atmospheric ion leakage.

procedure.title: Chamber Preparation and Environmental Desiccation
procedure.text: Inspect the torsion balance glass chamber and verify that the internal silica gel desiccant is active. Clean the insulating glass surfaces and quartz suspension rod with anhydrous ethanol, and verify that the relative humidity inside the chamber reads below 25%.
procedure.why: Water film condensation on insulating surfaces causes rapid electrostatic charge leakage by surface conduction, distorting force measurements.

procedure.title: Zero Balance and Torsion Wire Alignment
procedure.text: Adjust the leveling screws of the balance until the suspended dielectric beam swings freely without touching the chamber walls. Rotate the top torsion head dial until the index hair on the suspended sphere A aligns exactly with the chamber zero mark when both spheres are uncharged.
procedure.why: Eliminating mechanical zero-offset torque ensures that any angular twist observed during measurement is purely caused by electrostatic Coulomb forces.

procedure.title: Regulated Sphere Charging and Charge Verification
procedure.text: Connect the charging probe to the 3.0 kV regulated DC supply. Touch the probe simultaneously to the suspended sphere A and sliding sphere B while they are in contact, depositing an equal charge of q1 = q2 = 20.0 nC on both spheres. Verify the charge magnitude with the Faraday ice pail and electrometer.
procedure.why: Simultaneous contact charging of identical conducting spheres ensures strictly equal charge distribution (q1 = q2) by capacitive symmetry.

procedure.title: Coulomb Force Measurement vs Separation Distance
procedure.text: Advance the sliding carrier to position sphere B at a center-to-center separation distance of r = 4.0 cm from sphere A. As electrostatic repulsion deflects sphere A, rotate the torsion head dial until sphere A is restored precisely to its original zero mark. Record the restoring angle theta and calculate the electrostatic force F in micro-newtons.
procedure.why: The null-deflection restoration method maintains constant geometric orientation and lever arm length b, ensuring that the restoring torque kappa * theta is directly proportional to the Coulomb force F.

procedure.title: Systematic Separation Variation
procedure.text: Repeat the torsion null measurement for six discrete separation distances (r = 4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0, and 9.0 cm). For each station, record the separation distance r, the inverse square 1/r^2, and the measured repulsive force F.
procedure.why: Collecting data across a wide range of separations provides the necessary range of 1/r^2 to rigorously test the inverse-square law via linear regression.

procedure.title: Faraday Ice Pail and Charge Distribution Audit
procedure.text: Using the proof plane, sample the surface charge density from the sphere and transfer it into the Faraday ice pail to confirm zero interior charge and verify that total charge has not decayed significantly during the run.
procedure.why: Monitoring charge retention throughout the experiment confirms that charge leakage remained negligible and that Gauss's law conditions were maintained.

topics.title: Fundamental Electric Charges, Triboelectricity, and Electrostatic Induction
topics.text: All electrostatic phenomena arise from the microscopic atomic structure of matter, wherein negative electrons surround dense positive atomic nuclei. When two dissimilar insulating materials are brought into intimate microscopic contact, differential chemical electron affinities cause valence electrons to transfer across the interface—a phenomenon known as the triboelectric effect. In accordance with the fundamental law of charge conservation, the net electric charge in an isolated physical system remains strictly constant: charge is never created or destroyed, only transferred. Charges can be transferred between bodies via two distinct mechanisms: conduction and electrostatic induction. Conduction occurs through physical contact between a charged body and a neutral conductor, allowing mobile electrons to flow until electrical potentials equilibrate. In contrast, electrostatic induction redistributes mobile conduction electrons within a neutral conductor under the influence of an external Coulomb electric field without any physical contact. When a negatively charged rod is brought near an insulated neutral conductor, conduction electrons are repelled toward the far surface (free charge), leaving the near surface with a deficiency of electrons (bound positive charge). If the conductor is momentarily connected to Earth (grounded), the repelled free electrons drain into the reservoir of the Earth. Disconnecting the ground connection and subsequently removing the charged inducing rod leaves the conductor with a permanent, uniform net positive charge. Electrostatic induction proves that electrostatic forces act across space via electric fields and provides a contact-free method for charge generation.
topics.formula: Q_{\text{total}} = \sum q_i = \text{constant}, \qquad \vec{F} = q \vec{E}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{induced}} = \varepsilon_0 E_{\perp}
topics.question: Why can an insulated metal sphere be charged positively by induction using a negatively charged ebonite rod, without the rod losing any of its own charge?
topics.answer: During induction, the negative rod repels conduction electrons to the far side of the sphere. Grounding drains these free electrons to Earth. When the ground is removed and then the rod is taken away, the sphere is left with a deficiency of electrons (net positive charge). The rod never touches the sphere, so it transfers no charge and loses none of its own.

topics.title: Coulomb's Law, Field Equations, and the Inverse-Square Principle
topics.text: The quantitative foundation of electrostatics was established experimentally by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785. Coulomb formulated that the electrostatic force F acting between two stationary point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r in vacuum is directly proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = k_e (q₁ q₂ / r²), where the proportionality constant is Coulomb's constant k_e = 1 / (4πε₀) = 8.98755 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². The direction of the force is strictly along the line connecting the two charges: repulsive for charges of identical sign (q₁ q₂ > 0) and attractive for charges of opposite sign (q₁ q₂ < 0). In vector notation, the force exerted by charge q₁ on charge q₂ at position r₂ is: F₁₂ = [1 / (4πε₀)] [q₁ q₂ / |r₂ − r₁|²] r̂₁₂. Defining the electric field E as the electrostatic force per unit positive test charge (E = F / q₀), the field of a point charge is E = [1 / (4πε₀)] (q / r²) r̂. The inverse-square dependence on distance (1/r²) is a fundamental consequence of the three-dimensional geometry of space: the surface area of a spherical wavefront expands as 4πr², diluting the conserved flux of the electric field proportionally. Gauss's law, ∮ E · dA = Q_enc / ε₀, formalizes this conservation principle in integral form, while the differential form ∇ · E = ρ / ε₀ constitutes the first of Maxwell's four fundamental equations of electrodynamics.
topics.formula: \vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}, \qquad \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2} \hat{r}, \qquad \oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}
topics.question: How does the electrostatic force between two point charges change if both the charges and the distance between them are doubled?
topics.answer: From Coulomb's law F = k_e (q₁ q₂ / r²), doubling both charges quadruples the numerator (2 × 2 = 4), while doubling the distance quadruples the denominator (2² = 4). The factor of 4 cancels (4/4 = 1), leaving the electrostatic force completely unchanged.

topics.title: Coulomb's Torsion Balance Metrology and Finite-Size Corrections
topics.text: Because electrostatic forces between laboratory-scale charges (nanocoulombs) are exceptionally small (micro-newtons to milli-newtons), standard gravitational balance scales are inadequate. Coulomb overcame this measurement barrier by inventing the torsion balance. A thin, resilient vertical wire of length L_wire, radius r_wire, and shear modulus η suspends a light insulating rod carrying a charged conducting sphere of radius a at one end and a counterweight at the other. When a second identical charged sphere is placed nearby, electrostatic repulsion deflects the beam through an angle θ. By Hooke's law in torsion, twisting the suspension fiber by angle θ produces an elastic restoring torque: τ = κ θ, where κ = (π η r_wire⁴) / (2 L_wire) is the torsional constant of the fiber. In the null-restoration method, the experimenter rotates the top torsion head by angle θ until the suspended sphere returns exactly to its initial position. The restoring torque then balances the electrostatic torque: κ θ = F · b, where b is the moment arm from the suspension axis to the sphere center, directly yielding F = (κ / b) θ. In physical experiments, conducting spheres are not ideal mathematical point charges. When two conducting spheres of radius a are brought to separation r, mutual electrostatic induction redistributes surface charges toward the opposing poles. Lord Kelvin solved this boundary-value problem using the method of electrical images, deriving the series correction: F = F_point [1 − 4(a/r)³ + ...]. For spheres of radius a = 5.0 mm at distances r ≥ 40.0 mm, (a/r) ≤ 0.125, keeping finite-size departures below 0.7%.
topics.formula: \tau = \kappa \theta = F \cdot b \implies F = \frac{\kappa}{b} \theta, \qquad F_{\text{real}} \approx F_{\text{point}} \left[ 1 - 4\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^3 \right]
topics.question: Why is Coulomb's torsion balance vastly more sensitive for measuring minute electrostatic forces than a conventional spring balance?
topics.answer: A thin torsion fiber provides an extremely small mechanical restoring torque per unit twist angle (τ = κ θ, with κ ~ 10⁻⁸ N m/rad), allowing electrostatic forces in the micronewton (μN) regime to produce large, easily readable angular deflections of several degrees.

topics.title: Faraday's Ice-Pail Experiment, Electrostatic Shielding, and Gauss's Law
topics.text: In 1843, Michael Faraday conducted his renowned ice-pail experiment to elucidate the spatial distribution of electric charge and electrostatic shielding. An insulated hollow metal pail was connected to a sensitive gold-leaf electroscope. When a positively charged brass sphere suspended by a silk insulating thread was lowered into the interior of the pail without touching the walls, the electroscope leaves immediately diverged, indicating an induced charge. The positive charge on the sphere induced an equal and opposite negative charge (−Q) on the inner wall of the pail, and an equal positive charge (+Q) on the outer wall and electroscope leaves. When the sphere was moved around inside the pail, the electroscope divergence remained completely invariant, demonstrating that the external field depends only on total enclosed charge. When the sphere touched the inner bottom of the pail, the electroscope leaves did not move at all, and upon withdrawing the sphere, it was found to be completely discharged! All electric charge had migrated to the outer surface of the pail. Applying Gauss's law ∮ E · dA = Q_enc / ε₀ explains this fundamental result: inside the bulk metal of the pail, the electric field is strictly zero (E = 0). A Gaussian surface drawn within the metal enclosing the interior cavity must have zero net flux, proving that the charge on the inner wall is exactly equal and opposite to the charge on the sphere. When contact occurs, the inner charge is neutralized, and 100% of the charge resides on the outer surface. This phenomenon creates an electrostatic shield (Faraday cage), ensuring that interior electronic instruments are completely protected from external electrostatic fields.
topics.formula: \oint_{\text{cavity}} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0 \implies Q_{\text{inner}} = -Q_{\text{sphere}}, \qquad Q_{\text{outer}} = +Q_{\text{sphere}}, \qquad \vec{E}_{\text{interior}} = 0
topics.question: In Faraday's ice-pail experiment, why is no charge found on the inner surface of the metal pail after the charged sphere touches the inside?
topics.answer: By Gauss's law, like charges repel each other to the outermost boundary of a conductor to reach electrostatic equilibrium (minimum potential energy). When the sphere touches the interior wall, it becomes part of the interior cavity; all mobile charge flows instantly to the pail's outer surface, leaving the interior cavity with zero net charge and zero electric field.

topics.title: Surface Charge Distribution, Electric Field at a Conductor, and Corona Discharge
topics.text: For a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, mobile charges arrange themselves so that the tangential component of the electric field at the surface vanishes: E_parallel = 0. Consequently, the entire conducting body is an equipotential volume (V = constant). The electric field just outside the conducting surface is strictly normal to the surface, with a magnitude determined by Coulomb's boundary condition: E_perp = σ / ε₀, where σ is the local surface charge density. Using a proof plane—a small metallic disc on an insulating handle—experimentalists can sample the charge density σ at various points on charged conductors of different geometries. On a spherical conductor, symmetry enforces uniform charge distribution. However, on an irregular or pear-shaped conductor, surface charge density varies inversely with the local radius of curvature: σ ∝ 1 / R_curvature. At sharp points, edges, or needle tips where the radius of curvature approaches zero (R → 0), the surface charge density and electric field reach colossal values, easily exceeding the dielectric breakdown strength of dry air (E_breakdown ≈ 3.0 × 10⁶ V/m = 30 kV/cm). When this threshold is crossed, the intense field accelerates ambient electrons, initiating Townsend avalanche ionization. Gas molecules are dissociated into glowing plasma (corona discharge), generating positive ions that are violently repelled from the tip. This stream of accelerated ions creates a detectable aerodynamic draft known as 'electric wind', capable of blowing out candle flames or spinning reaction pinwheels.
topics.formula: \vec{E}_{\text{surface}} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \hat{n}, \qquad \sigma \propto \frac{1}{R_{\text{curvature}}}, \qquad E_{\text{breakdown}} \approx 3.0 \times 10^6 \text{ V m}^{-1}
topics.question: Why does electrostatic charge concentrate at sharp points and edges rather than distributing uniformly over an irregularly shaped conductor?
topics.answer: On an equipotential conducting surface, the electric field is inversely proportional to the local radius of curvature (E ∝ 1/R). At sharp points (where R → 0), the surface charge density σ = ε₀ E becomes enormous to maintain uniform potential throughout the body.

topics.title: Linear Regression Formulation and OLS Parameter Isolation
topics.text: To determine Coulomb's constant k_e and the permittivity of free space ε₀ without relying on isolated, error-prone single measurements, experimentalists record the repulsive force F across a systematic series of separation distances r (e.g. 4.0 to 9.0 cm). From Coulomb's inverse-square law F = k_e q₁ q₂ (1/r²), defining x = 1/r² (in m⁻²) as the independent variable and y = F (in N) as the dependent variable transforms the non-linear physical law into the canonical linear regression model: y = m x + b. Here, the regression slope m represents the product of Coulomb's constant and the sphere charges: m = k_e q₁ q₂. For identical sphere charges (q₁ = q₂ = q), the slope becomes m = k_e q². Inverting this relationship isolates Coulomb's constant directly: k_e = m / q². Furthermore, the permittivity of free space is obtained from k_e = 1 / (4πε₀) as: ε₀ = 1 / (4π k_e) = q² / (4π m). The regression intercept b provides an indispensable experimental diagnostic: theoretically b = 0, so any statistically significant non-zero intercept detects zero-offset fiber twist, residual stray charges on the chamber walls, or unmodelled image charge forces. Ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression minimizes the sum of squared force residuals, averaging out random torsion sighting errors and providing rigorous standard error evaluations for both slope and intercept.
topics.formula: F = m \left(\frac{1}{r^2}\right) + b \implies m = k_e q^2 \iff k_e = \frac{m}{q^2}, \qquad \varepsilon_0 = \frac{1}{4\pi k_e} = \frac{q^2}{4\pi m}
topics.question: When plotting electrostatic force F on the vertical axis against 1/r² on the horizontal axis, what does the regression slope m represent?
topics.answer: The slope m = F / (1/r²) equals the electrostatic force constant product: m = k_e q₁ q₂ = (q₁ q₂) / (4πε₀). Dividing the slope by the known product of the charges q² directly yields Coulomb's constant k_e = m / q².

topics.title: Dielectric Polarization, Relative Permittivity (κ), and Modern Applications
topics.text: When an insulating material (dielectric) is introduced into an electrostatic field, the charges within its atoms and molecules cannot move freely like conduction electrons. Instead, the external field induces microscopic dielectric polarization: positive atomic nuclei are displaced slightly in the direction of the field, while negative electron clouds shift in the opposite direction, forming microscopic electric dipoles. In polar dielectrics (such as water molecules), permanent dipoles undergo partial rotational alignment. The macroscopic alignment of these microscopic dipoles is quantified by the polarization vector P = ε₀ (κ − 1) E, where κ = ε_r is the dimensionless relative permittivity (dielectric constant). This internal polarization produces bound surface charges (σ_p = P · n̂) that generate an internal depolarizing field opposing the applied field. Consequently, the net electric field inside the dielectric is reduced by a factor of κ: E = E₀ / κ, and the electrostatic force between charges embedded in the dielectric is attenuated: F = (1 / 4πε₀κ) (q₁ q₂ / r²). In vacuum or dry air, κ ≈ 1.0006; in glass, κ ≈ 5 to 10; and in pure water, κ ≈ 80.1. Modern electrostatics exploits these principles in industrial electrostatic precipitators that capture 99.9% of particulate soot from power plant exhausts, xerographic laser printing and photocopying using photoconductive selenium drums, electrostatic powder coating of automobile chassis, capacitive touchscreen sensors, and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) profiling work functions at atomic resolution.
topics.formula: \vec{P} = \varepsilon_0 (\kappa - 1) \vec{E}, \qquad \vec{E} = \frac{\vec{E}_0}{\kappa}, \qquad F_{\text{dielectric}} = \frac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 \kappa} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} = \frac{F_{\text{vacuum}}}{\kappa}
topics.question: If two charges are submerged in pure water (dielectric constant κ = 80) at the same separation distance, how does the electrostatic force between them compare to their force in air?
topics.answer: The force in water is reduced by a factor of 80: F_water = F_air / κ = F_air / 80. Molecular water dipoles orient themselves around the charges, producing a strong polarization screening field that counteracts the original Coulomb field.

quiz.question: According to Coulomb's law, if the separation distance between two charged conducting spheres is reduced to one-third of its original value, the electrostatic repulsive force becomes:
options: 9 times greater
3 times greater
One-third of the original force
27 times greater
quiz.explanation: Coulomb's force is inversely proportional to the square of distance: F ∝ 1/r². Reducing r by a factor of 3 increases F by a factor of 1 / (1/3)² = 9.

quiz.question: In Faraday's ice-pail experiment, touching a charged sphere to the inner surface of an insulated hollow metal container causes:
options: All charge to transfer entirely to the outer surface of the container
Equal division of charge between the sphere and the inner container wall
The container to lose all electrical charge to the atmosphere
The electric field inside the hollow container to increase significantly
quiz.explanation: Under electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge on a conductor resides exclusively on its outer surface. Touching the inside makes the sphere part of the cavity; all charge migrates to the outer surface, leaving the inside with zero charge and zero electric field.

quiz.question: If the regression slope of electrostatic force F plotted against 1/r² is m = 3.595 × 10⁻⁶ N m², and each sphere carries a charge of 20.0 nC, what is the value of Coulomb's constant k_e?
options: 8.988 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
4.494 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²
1.798 × 10¹⁰ N m² C⁻²
8.854 × 10⁻¹² N m² C⁻²

quiz.question: What happens when an uncharged, insulated conductor is grounded while under the influence of an adjacent positive electric charge?
options: Electrons flow from Earth onto the conductor, neutralizing the free positive charge
Positive charge flows from the conductor into Earth, leaving it neutral
The bound negative charge escapes into Earth
The conductor acquires a net positive charge equal to the inducing body
quiz.explanation: The positive inducing body attracts negative conduction electrons to the near side (bound charge) and repels positive charge to the far side (free charge). Grounding allows electrons from Earth to flow in and neutralize the free charge. When ground is disconnected, a net negative charge remains.

precautions: Ground all outer metallic shielding cases and observer wrist straps before operating the balance to prevent stray electrostatic induction from clothing or body capacitance.
Never breathe directly toward the open balance chamber, as moisture in exhaled breath instantly compromises the high-insulation quartz surfaces.
Ensure the separation distance r is always at least 4 times the sphere radius (r >= 4a) to keep finite-size multipole induction corrections below 0.7%.
Approach the null reading position slowly to avoid setting the suspended torsion beam into persistent rotational swinging.
limitations: The analytical model treats the conducting spheres as mathematical point charges in an infinite, unbounded vacuum, neglecting electrostatic image charges induced in the chamber walls, minor finite-size multipole surface charge redistribution (Lord Kelvin image correction ~0.3% at r = 4 cm), and residual atmospheric ion leakage (~0.1 nC/min). In a physical laboratory, slight fiber mechanical hysteresis (zero drift after large twists), minute convective air currents inside the glass chamber, and environmental humidity fluctuations introduce small experimental scatter.

title: Magnetic Fields: Tangent Galvanometer, Biot-Savart Law, and Earth's Horizontal Magnetic Component
subject: physics
aim: To investigate the magnetic field generated by an electric current in a circular coil, verify the Biot-Savart law and tangent law of magnetism, observe magnetic torque equilibrium on a compass needle, and determine the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field (B_H) and the reduction factor using linear regression.
intro: The discovery by Hans Christian Ørsted in 1820 that an electric current deflects a magnetic needle inaugurated the unified science of electromagnetism. Soon after, Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart formulated the fundamental law governing the magnetic field dB produced by an infinitesimal current element I dℓ: dB = (μ₀ / 4π) [I (dℓ × r̂) / r²], where μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ is the permeability of free space. Integrating this fundamental relation around a flat circular coil of N turns and mean radius R carrying direct current I establishes an axial magnetic field at the coil's geometric center: B_coil = (μ₀ N I) / (2R) = G I, where G = (μ₀ N) / (2R) is the geometric coil constant. In the tangent galvanometer, this circular coil is mounted vertically with its plane aligned strictly in the magnetic meridian—parallel to the horizontal component of Earth's geomagnetic field B_H. At the exact center of the coil, a small magnetic compass needle is pivoted on a low-friction jewel bearing. When direct current passes through the windings, the needle experiences two mutually orthogonal magnetic fields: Earth's horizontal field B_H along the plane of the coil, and the current's magnetic field B_coil perpendicular to the coil plane. Under the action of these orthogonal fields, the needle experiences opposing magnetic torques: τ_coil = M B_coil cos θ and τ_Earth = M B_H sin θ, where M is the magnetic dipole moment of the needle and θ is the angular deflection. Equating these torques establishes the celebrated tangent law of magnetism: B_coil = B_H tan θ. Substituting the Biot-Savart expression yields: (μ₀ N I) / (2R) = B_H tan θ, which rearranges to tan θ = [μ₀ N / (2 R B_H)] I, or I = [2 R B_H / (μ₀ N)] tan θ = K tan θ, where K = B_H / G is the reduction factor of the galvanometer. By systematically varying the current I using a rheostat and measuring the resulting deflection angle θ across four quadrant orientations using an anti-parallax mirror and a reversing commutator, students cancel zero-offset and alignment errors. Ordinary least-squares regression of tan θ against current I yields a straight line whose slope m = G / B_H isolates Earth's horizontal field B_H = G / m with remarkable precision, confirming the foundations of electromagnetic force, geomagnetic field metrology, and Ampère's circulating currents.
fitEquation: \tan\theta = \left(\frac{\mu_0 N}{2 R B_H}\right) I \iff y = m x + b \iff B_H = \frac{\mu_0 N}{2 R m}, \quad K = \frac{1}{m}
settings: Ambient room temperature: T = 20.0 °C; Reference Earth horizontal field: B_H = 3.500 × 10⁻⁵ T (35.00 μT).
Galvanometer coil: N = 50 turns of insulated copper wire (mean radius R = 10.00 cm).
Coil magnetic constant: G = μ₀ N / (2R) = 3.14159 × 10⁻⁴ T A⁻¹.
Galvanometer reduction factor: K = B_H / G = 0.11141 A (111.4 mA).
Magnetic needle: High-coercivity cobalt steel needle (length 2ℓ = 15.0 mm ≪ 2R) with jeweled pivot.
Permeability of free space: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ = 1.256637 × 10⁻⁶ T m A⁻¹.

apparatus.name: Stewart & Gee Tangent Galvanometer
apparatus.purpose: Precision instrument with 50-turn vertical circular copper coil (mean radius R = 10.0 cm), brass leveling tripod with leveling screws, and central compass box with 360° protractor scale and anti-parallax mirror.

apparatus.name: Pohl Current Reversing Commutator
apparatus.purpose: Heavy-duty four-terminal rocker commutator allowing rapid, arc-free reversal of current direction through the galvanometer coil without disturbing circuit connections.

apparatus.name: Regulated DC Power Supply
apparatus.purpose: Low-noise variable DC voltage supply (0 to 12.0 V, 2 A) equipped with digital voltage and current monitoring.

apparatus.name: Precision Decade Resistance Box / Slide-Wire Rheostat
apparatus.purpose: Non-inductive wire-wound rheostat (0 to 100 Ω, 2 A rating) for smooth, continuous adjustment of coil current.

apparatus.name: Digital Multimeter / Precision Ammeter
apparatus.purpose: Calibrated 4½-digit true-RMS digital ammeter (0.1 mA resolution) to verify current readings against galvanometer deflections.

apparatus.name: Magnetic Dip Needle and Compass
apparatus.purpose: Freely suspended dip circle for determining the local magnetic meridian and measuring inclination angle.

procedure.title: Leveling and Magnetic Meridian Alignment
procedure.text: Place the tangent galvanometer on a rigid, non-magnetic wooden bench away from iron fixtures or DC power leads. Using the leveling screws, level the base until the central compass needle swings freely. Rotate the coil until its vertical plane is exactly parallel to the compass needle pointing North-South (0°–0° alignment).
procedure.why: The tangent law B_coil = B_H tan θ requires the coil's axial magnetic field to be strictly orthogonal to Earth's horizontal field.

procedure.title: Circuit Wiring and Commutator Connection
procedure.text: Connect the DC power supply in series with the rheostat, precision ammeter, reversing commutator, and the 50-turn coil terminals. Inspect all connections to verify tight, clean non-magnetic contacts.
procedure.why: Series connection ensures identical current flows through the ammeter and galvanometer coil, while the commutator enables bilateral deflection testing.

procedure.title: Current Adjustment and Forward Deflection Recording
procedure.text: Turn on the power supply and adjust the rheostat until a current of I = 50.0 mA flows through the coil. Using the anti-parallax mirror (aligning the pointer with its image), record the deflection angle θ1 on both ends of the aluminum pointer (East and West tips).
procedure.why: Reading both ends of the pointer eliminates error caused by the pointer pivot not being at the exact center of the graduated scale.

procedure.title: Commutation and Reversed Deflection Recording
procedure.text: Throw the reversing commutator to reverse the current direction through the coil without altering the rheostat. Record the deflection angle θ2 at both ends of the pointer on the opposite side of the scale, and calculate the mean deflection θ = (θ1 + θ2) / 2.
procedure.why: Reversing current cancels out zero-offset pointer bending, residual coil tilt, and minor magnetic meridian alignment errors.

procedure.title: Systematic Current Variation
procedure.text: Repeat the four-reading measurement sequence for six discrete current levels (50.0, 80.0, 110.0, 140.0, 170.0, and 200.0 mA). Record current I in mA and calculate tan θ for each station.
procedure.why: Varying current over the optimum deflection range (24° to 61°) provides robust data for linear regression, yielding an accurate slope.

procedure.title: Coil Dimension Verification
procedure.text: Measure the inner and outer diameters of the circular coil using vernier calipers to compute the mean radius R = 10.0 cm, and confirm the turn count N = 50.
procedure.why: Accurate knowledge of coil geometry is essential to calculate the coil constant G = μ₀ N / (2R) and isolate Earth's horizontal field B_H.

topics.title: The Biot-Savart Law and Magnetic Fields of Electric Currents
topics.text: The quantitative law governing magnetic fields produced by electric currents was deduced empirically by Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart in 1820. For an infinitesimal filamentary current element I dℓ carrying steady electric current I, the differential magnetic field dB at a field point located at position vector r relative to the element is given by: dB = (μ₀ / 4π) [I (dℓ × r̂) / r²], where μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ is the magnetic permeability of free space. To evaluate the magnetic field produced at the center of a flat circular coil of radius R having N tightly wound turns, we integrate around the circumference. At every point on the circle, the current tangent vector dℓ is perpendicular to the radial vector r̂ (dℓ · r̂ = 0, |dℓ × r̂| = dℓ). Since every element is at the constant distance r = R, the integral evaluates as: B_center = (μ₀ N I / 4π R²) ∮ dℓ = (μ₀ N I / 4π R²) (2πR) = (μ₀ N I) / (2R). The direction of the magnetic field vector is strictly normal to the plane of the coil, directed along the coil axis in accordance with the right-hand grip rule (curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of conventional current leaves the thumb pointing along the magnetic field). Defining the magnetic coil constant G = (μ₀ N) / (2R), the central field is simply B_coil = G I. Along the central axis at distance z from the coil plane, the field diminishes according to the axial formula: B_z(z) = [μ₀ N I R²] / [2 (R² + z²)³/²]. At large distances (z ≫ R), this expression simplifies to the dipole field B_z ≈ (μ₀ / 4π) (2m / z³), where m = N I A = N I (π R²) is the magnetic dipole moment of the coil.
topics.formula: d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{I (d\vec{\ell} \times \hat{r})}{r^2}, \qquad B_{\text{center}} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R} = G I, \qquad B_z(z) = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2 (R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}
topics.question: Why does the magnetic field at the center of a circular coil increase linearly with the number of turns N?
topics.answer: By the principle of linear superposition in magnetostatics, each individual turn carries the same current I in the same rotational direction, contributing an identical magnetic field dB = μ₀ I / (2R). Summing over N closely wound turns yields B = N (μ₀ I / (2R)) = μ₀ N I / (2R).

topics.title: The Tangent Law of Magnetism and Galvanometer Metrology
topics.text: The operational principle of the tangent galvanometer is based on the tangent law of magnetism, which governs the equilibrium orientation of a magnetic compass needle subjected to two orthogonal magnetic fields. Let a small magnetic needle of magnetic dipole moment M and pole strength p be freely pivoted at its center on an agate jewel bearing. When the coil of the galvanometer is aligned with its plane parallel to the magnetic meridian, Earth's horizontal magnetic field B_H exerts a restoring torque on the needle that attempts to align it with magnetic North: τ_Earth = M B_H sin θ, where θ is the deflection angle away from the meridian. Simultaneously, when direct current I passes through the coil windings, it produces an axial magnetic field B_coil strictly perpendicular to the magnetic meridian (directed East-West). This coil field exerts a deflecting torque on the needle: τ_coil = M B_coil cos θ. In static equilibrium, the two opposing torques must balance exactly: M B_coil cos θ = M B_H sin θ. Dividing both sides by M cos θ yields the tangent law: B_coil = B_H tan θ. Substituting the Biot-Savart expression B_coil = (μ₀ N I) / (2R) gives: (μ₀ N I) / (2R) = B_H tan θ. Rearranging for current I yields: I = [2 R B_H / (μ₀ N)] tan θ = K tan θ, where K = (2 R B_H) / (μ₀ N) is called the reduction factor of the tangent galvanometer. The reduction factor K represents the specific current required to produce an angular deflection of exactly 45° (since tan 45° = 1). For the tangent law to remain strictly valid, the needle must be short compared to the coil radius (2ℓ ≪ R) so that its poles remain within the uniform central field zone.
topics.formula: B_{\text{coil}} = B_H \tan\theta \iff \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R} = B_H \tan\theta \implies I = K \tan\theta, \quad K = \frac{2 R B_H}{\mu_0 N} = \frac{B_H}{G}
topics.question: Why must the compass needle at the center of a tangent galvanometer be very short in comparison to the diameter of the coil?
topics.answer: The Biot-Savart formula B = μ₀ N I / (2R) holds strictly at the exact geometric center of the coil. A short needle (length ≪ R) ensures that both magnetic poles remain entirely within the uniform central field region without experiencing non-uniform field gradients near the wire turns.

topics.title: Earth's Geomagnetic Field and the Magnetic Meridian
topics.text: Earth acts as a giant magnetic dipole tilted at an angle of approximately 11.3° relative to its rotational axis, generated by turbulent magnetohydrodynamic convection of molten iron and nickel in the outer core (the geodynamo). At any point on Earth's surface, the total geomagnetic field vector B can be decomposed into two orthogonal components: a horizontal component B_H directed along the local magnetic meridian toward the magnetic North pole, and a vertical component B_V directed downward into the Earth in the Northern Hemisphere (or upward in the Southern Hemisphere). The angle that the total field vector makes with the horizontal plane is the magnetic dip (inclination angle I_d), related by: tan I_d = B_V / B_H, with B = √(B_H² + B_V²). At the magnetic equator, B_V = 0 and I_d = 0°, so the entire field is horizontal; at the magnetic poles, B_H = 0 and I_d = 90°, so the field is purely vertical. In tangent galvanometer measurements, only the horizontal component B_H acts on the horizontally pivoted compass needle, because the vertical component B_V exerts a vertical downward force that is absorbed by the mechanical reaction of the jewel pivot. The magnetic meridian is the vertical plane passing through the magnetic North and South poles at the observation site. Aligning the vertical plane of the galvanometer coil precisely parallel to the magnetic meridian is an absolute prerequisite: if the coil is misaligned by angle α, the coil field is no longer perpendicular to B_H, distorting the tangent relation into tan θ = (B_coil cos α) / (B_H ± B_coil sin α).
topics.formula: \vec{B} = \vec{B}_H + \vec{B}_V, \qquad \tan I_d = \frac{B_V}{B_H}, \qquad B = \sqrt{B_H^2 + B_V^2}, \qquad B_H \approx 3.50 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}
topics.question: Why must the plane of the tangent galvanometer coil be aligned strictly parallel to the magnetic meridian before taking measurements?
topics.answer: The tangent law (B_coil = B_H tan θ) requires the magnetic field of the coil B_coil to be strictly perpendicular to Earth's horizontal field B_H. Aligning the coil plane in the magnetic meridian ensures B_coil (which is perpendicular to the coil plane) is exactly orthogonal to B_H.

topics.title: Galvanometer Sensitivity and the Optimum Deflection Window
topics.text: The precision of a tangent galvanometer depends strongly on the angular deflection θ at which readings are collected. The absolute current sensitivity S_I is defined as the change in angular deflection per unit change in current: S_I = dθ / dI. Differentiating the tangent relation I = K tan θ with respect to θ yields: dI / dθ = K sec² θ, so S_I = dθ / dI = 1 / (K sec² θ) = (cos² θ) / K. This shows that the absolute sensitivity is highest near zero deflection (cos 0° = 1) and drops to zero as θ approaches 90°. However, experimentalists are primarily concerned with minimizing the relative fractional error in current measurement: dI / I. Dividing dI = K sec² θ dθ by I = K tan θ yields: dI / I = (sec² θ / tan θ) dθ = [1 / (sin θ cos θ)] dθ = [2 / sin 2θ] dθ. To minimize the fractional current error dI / I for a given pointer reading resolution dθ, the denominator sin 2θ must be maximized. The sine function reaches its absolute maximum of 1 when 2θ = 90°, which corresponds to an optimum deflection angle of θ = 45°. At θ = 45°, dI / I = 2 dθ. In contrast, for very small deflections (e.g. θ = 10°, sin 20° = 0.342), dI / I = 5.85 dθ (nearly three times worse); for large deflections (e.g. θ = 80°, sin 160° = 0.342), dI / I is similarly degraded. Therefore, rigorous laboratory protocol dictates adjusting the series rheostat so that galvanometer deflections fall strictly within the optimum window between 30° and 60° (where sin 2θ ≥ 0.866).
topics.formula: S_I = \frac{d\theta}{dI} = \frac{\cos^2\theta}{K}, \qquad \frac{dI}{I} = \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta} d\theta \implies \left(\frac{dI}{I}\right)_{\text{min}} \iff \theta = 45^\circ
topics.question: At what deflection angle θ does a tangent galvanometer have maximum fractional current measurement accuracy, and why?
topics.answer: Maximum accuracy occurs at θ = 45°. The fractional current error is dI / I = (2 / sin 2θ) dθ, which reaches its minimum when sin 2θ is maximized (sin 2θ = 1 at 2θ = 90°, hence θ = 45°).

topics.title: Commutation, Parallax Elimination, and Systematic Error Cancellation
topics.text: High-accuracy magnetic measurements require systematic cancellation of mechanical, optical, and orientation artifacts. The tangent galvanometer incorporates three primary metrological safeguards: bilateral pointer reading, an anti-parallax mirror, and a Pohl current reversing commutator. First, the compass needle carries a long, lightweight aluminum pointer mounted perpendicular to the magnetic needle. Both ends of the pointer are read on the circular protractor scale (East and West tips). Averaging the two tips cancels any eccentricity error arising from the jeweled pivot not being situated at the exact geometric center of the degree circle. Second, beneath the glass window of the compass box lies a concentric plane mirror ring. When taking a reading, the observer must position their eye so that the fine tip of the pointer directly covers its own optical reflection in the mirror, eliminating sighting parallax error. Third, a Pohl four-terminal commutator switch is connected in the circuit. After recording readings for direct current flow (θ₁), the commutator is thrown to invert current through the coil, causing the needle to deflect in the opposite direction (θ₂). Averaging the four pointer readings [θ = (θ₁_left + θ₁_right + θ₂_left + θ₂_right) / 4] cancels: (1) any zero-offset bending of the aluminum pointer, (2) residual leveling tilt of the coil, and (3) small residual angular misalignment between the coil plane and the magnetic meridian.
topics.formula: \theta = \frac{\theta_{1,\text{east}} + \theta_{1,\text{west}} + \theta_{2,\text{east}} + \theta_{2,\text{west}}}{4}, \qquad \delta\theta_{\text{parallax}} \to 0, \qquad \delta\theta_{\text{eccentricity}} \to 0
topics.question: Why is a current reversing commutator used to take readings with both direct and reversed currents in each trial?
topics.answer: Reversing the current and reading both ends of the pointer across four positions cancels out: (1) pointer zero-offset bending error, (2) residual coil leveling tilt, and (3) minor misalignment between the coil plane and the magnetic meridian.

topics.title: Linear Regression Formulation and OLS Parameter Isolation
topics.text: To determine Earth's horizontal field B_H and the galvanometer reduction factor K with statistical rigor, experimentalists vary the coil current I across a calibrated series (e.g. 50.0 to 200.0 mA) and measure the corresponding mean deflection angle θ. From the fundamental tangent relation tan θ = [μ₀ N / (2 R B_H)] I, designating current x = I (in amperes) as the independent variable and y = tan θ (dimensionless) as the dependent variable transforms the physical law into the canonical linear regression model: y = m x + b. Here, the regression slope m represents the ratio of the geometric coil constant G to Earth's horizontal field: m = G / B_H = (μ₀ N) / (2 R B_H). Inverting this relation isolates Earth's horizontal field directly: B_H = G / m = (μ₀ N) / (2 R m). Furthermore, the reduction factor of the galvanometer is simply the reciprocal of the regression slope: K = 1 / m. The regression intercept b serves as an indispensable diagnostic: theoretically b = 0, so any statistically significant non-zero intercept detects residual magnetic fields from nearby DC wiring, uncompensated stray iron magnetization, or imperfect commutator symmetry. Ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression minimizes the sum of squared tangent residuals, averaging out random pointer sighting errors and providing unbiased slope and standard error estimates.
topics.formula: \tan\theta = m I + b \implies m = \frac{\mu_0 N}{2 R B_H} = \frac{G}{B_H} \iff B_H = \frac{\mu_0 N}{2 R m}, \qquad K = \frac{1}{m}
topics.question: When plotting tan θ on the vertical axis against current I on the horizontal axis, what does the regression slope m represent?
topics.answer: The slope m = tan θ / I equals the coil constant divided by Earth's horizontal field: m = G / B_H = (μ₀ N) / (2 R B_H). Dividing the known coil constant G by the slope m directly isolates Earth's horizontal field B_H = G / m.

topics.title: Helmholtz Coils, Magnetic Shielding, and Modern Applications
topics.text: While a single circular coil produces a localized magnetic field that falls off rapidly along the axis (B ∝ 1 / z³), Hermann von Helmholtz demonstrated in 1849 that pairing two identical coaxial circular coils separated by an axial distance equal to their radius (d = R) creates an extraordinarily uniform magnetic field throughout the central inter-coil volume. Expanding the axial magnetic field in a Taylor series about the central midpoint (z = 0), symmetry ensures that all odd derivatives vanish: dB/dz = 0, d³B/dz³ = 0. By choosing the coil separation d = R, the second derivative also vanishes identically: d²B/dz² = 0. Consequently, the first non-zero spatial variation occurs at the fourth derivative (d⁴B/dz⁴), providing a uniform magnetic field volume with spatial homogeneity exceeding 99.9%. Today, Helmholtz and Maxwell coil systems are essential tools in modern science and engineering: they are used to cancel Earth's magnetic field in magnetically shielded cleanrooms for atomic clock fountain experiments, calibrate fluxgate and atomic optical magnetometers on space exploration probes, test magnetometers for aerospace guidance, and provide homogeneous bias fields in electron spin resonance (ESR) and low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
topics.formula: B_{\text{Helmholtz}} = \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{3/2} \frac{\mu_0 N I}{R} \approx 0.7155 \frac{\mu_0 N I}{R}, \qquad \left.\frac{d^2 B_z}{dz^2}\right|_{z=0} = 0 \iff d = R
topics.question: How does the Helmholtz coil configuration improve upon the single circular coil of a tangent galvanometer?
topics.answer: Helmholtz coils place two identical coils of radius R separated by distance d = R. This geometry makes both the first and second spatial derivatives of the axial field vanish (dB/dz = 0 and d²B/dz² = 0) at the center, creating an extremely uniform magnetic field over a much larger volume.

quiz.question: In a tangent galvanometer, the plane of the circular coil must be oriented:
options: Parallel to the magnetic meridian (along Earth's horizontal magnetic field)
Perpendicular to the magnetic meridian (East-West)
Inclined at an angle of 45° to the magnetic meridian
Horizontally flat on the bench
quiz.explanation: The plane of the coil must lie parallel to the magnetic meridian so that the magnetic field produced by the current (which is axial, perpendicular to the coil) is strictly orthogonal to Earth's horizontal magnetic field, satisfying the tangent law.

quiz.question: According to the tangent law of magnetism, when a compass needle deflects by angle θ under the influence of coil field B_coil and Earth's horizontal field B_H:
options: B_coil = B_H tan θ
B_coil = B_H sin θ
B_coil = B_H cos θ
B_coil = B_H cot θ
quiz.explanation: Equating the opposing torques M B_coil cos θ = M B_H sin θ yields B_coil / B_H = sin θ / cos θ = tan θ, so B_coil = B_H tan θ.

quiz.question: If a tangent galvanometer has a reduction factor K = 0.1114 A, what current is required to produce an optimum deflection of θ = 45°?
At what deflection angle θ is the tangent galvanometer most sensitive to small changes in current?
options: 0° (where cos² θ is maximum)
45° (where sin 2θ is maximum)
90° (where tan θ is infinite)
60° (where sec θ = 2)
quiz.explanation: The absolute angular sensitivity dθ/dI = (cos² θ) / K is maximal at θ = 0° (where cos 0° = 1). Note that the relative fractional precision dI/I is best at 45°, but absolute angular rate dθ/dI is greatest near 0°.

precautions: Ensure no ferromagnetic objects (iron stands, steel screwdrivers, cell phones, or transformer cores) are within 1.5 meters of the apparatus to prevent stray magnetic distortion.
Align the aluminum pointer tip with its reflection in the mirror ring directly beneath it to eliminate visual parallax when reading the degree scale.
Keep currents below 300 mA to prevent resistive Joule heating of the copper coil, which would alter coil dimensions and wire resistance.
Always reverse current and average all four pointer readings (both ends, both polarities) for every observation station.
limitations: The analytical model treats the magnetic needle as an infinitesimal point dipole situated at the exact geometric center of the circular coil, assumes perfectly uniform coil windings with negligible axial width, and treats Earth's magnetic field as strictly stationary and uniform. In a physical laboratory, finite needle length introduces a small second-order correction (1 + 0.75 (ℓ/R)² (5 cos² θ − 1) ≈ 0.2%), building structural steel reinforcement produces localized geomagnetic distortion, and diurnal solar geomagnetic drift causes minor baseline fluctuations (~0.1 μT).

title: Electric Fields: Equipotential Mapping, Electric Field Lines, and Potential Gradient
subject: physics
aim: To investigate the electrostatic potential distribution in a two-dimensional conducting medium for uniform parallel-plate and non-uniform dipole electrode configurations, map equipotential contours, verify the strict spatial orthogonality between electric field lines and equipotential surfaces, measure the electric potential gradient (E = −dV/dx), and determine the uniform electric field strength using ordinary least-squares linear regression.
intro: The concept of the electric field, first introduced by Michael Faraday, provides an indispensable spatial framework for describing electromagnetic interactions across space. At every point in an electrostatic field, the electric field vector E is defined as the force F exerted per unit positive test charge q₀: E = F / q₀. In static conditions, Coulomb's force is strictly conservative, meaning the line integral of electric force along any closed path vanishes identically: ∮ E · dℓ = 0. Consequently, the electric field can be expressed rigorously as the negative gradient of a scalar electrostatic potential function V(r): E = −∇V = −(∂V/∂x î + ∂V/∂y ĵ + ∂V/∂z k̂). The scalar potential difference between two arbitrary spatial coordinates A and B represents the external work required to transport a unit positive charge from A to B against the electric field: V_B − V_A = −∫_A^B E · dℓ. An equipotential surface is defined as the locus of all contiguous points in space having the exact same electrostatic potential V. If a test charge is displaced along an equipotential surface by a differential displacement dℓ, no electrostatic work is performed: dW = −q₀ (E · dℓ) = −q₀ dV = 0. Because dV = 0 and |E| ≠ 0, it follows from the scalar product E · dℓ = |E| |dℓ| cos θ = 0 that cos θ = 0, which dictates θ = 90°. Hence, electric field lines are everywhere strictly perpendicular to equipotential surfaces. In a direct experimental laboratory, mapping static electric fields in a pure dielectric medium is notoriously challenging due to parasitic atmospheric ion neutralization and surface charge leakage. However, by virtue of the exact mathematical correspondence between electrostatics and steady direct current flow in a uniform conducting sheet (Ohm's law in point form: J = σ E, combined with current continuity ∇ · J = 0 in charge-free regions yielding Laplace's equation ∇²V = 0), the potential distribution in a thin conducting paper (such as carbon-impregnated Teledeltos paper of uniform surface resistivity R_s) is mathematically identical to the electrostatic field in a dielectric. When two parallel linear brass electrodes of length L separated by distance d are energized with a constant DC potential difference V₀, the electric field in the central inter-electrode region is remarkably uniform: E = V₀ / d = const. Along the symmetry axis perpendicular to the plates, the potential varies linearly with displacement x measured from the grounded electrode (V = 0 at x = 0): V(x) = (V₀ / d) x = E x. In contrast, for curved or dipole electrode geometries, field lines flare outwards and equipotential lines curve into families of orthogonal circular arcs and hyperbolas, concentrating potential gradients near points of high surface curvature. By systematically measuring the potential V at calibrated spatial positions x using a high-impedance digital voltmeter and point-contact tracking probes, students obtain an empirical dataset that maps equipotentials, constructs orthogonal flux lines, and applies ordinary least-squares linear regression (V = m x + b) to determine the uniform electric field strength E = m with rigorous metrological precision.
fitEquation: V(x) = E x + b \iff y = m x + b \implies E = m, \quad b \to 0.000 \text{ V}
settings: Applied electrode potential difference: V₀ = 10.00 V DC; Reference uniform electric field: E = V₀ / d = 100.00 V m⁻¹.
Electrode geometry: Dual parallel brass bar electrodes (length L = 20.00 cm, inter-electrode gap d = 10.00 cm = 0.100 m).
Conducting sheet substrate: High-uniformity carbon-impregnated Teledeltos paper (surface resistivity R_s = 2000 Ω/□).
Measurement instrumentation: 4½-digit true-RMS digital voltmeter (input impedance Z_in = 10.0 MΩ, resolution 1 mV).
Point tracking probe: Spring-loaded copper-beryllium tracking probe with hardened contact tip (radius r_tip = 0.5 mm).
Ambient laboratory environment: Temperature T = 20.0 °C, relative humidity RH = 45% (controlled non-condensing atmosphere).

apparatus.name: Teledeltos Conducting Paper Mapping Board
apparatus.purpose: Precision insulated mounting board supporting a 30 cm × 40 cm sheet of uniform carbon-graphite conducting paper, underlaid with a transparent 1 mm metric Cartesian coordinate grid for high-precision probe tracking.

apparatus.name: Parallel Linear Brass Electrodes
apparatus.purpose: Pair of matched, heavy machined brass bar electrodes (length L = 20.0 cm, width 1.0 cm, thickness 0.5 cm) clamped securely onto the conducting paper with colloidal silver conductive paint to establish uniform parallel equipotential boundaries.

apparatus.name: Regulated Variable DC Power Supply
apparatus.purpose: Low-noise laboratory DC power supply (0 to 15.00 V, 1.0 A current limit) providing an ultra-stable 10.00 V potential difference across the boundary electrodes.

apparatus.name: High-Impedance Digital Voltmeter (DVM)
apparatus.purpose: Digital multimeter with 10.0 MΩ input resistance and 1 mV voltage resolution, designed to sample local surface potentials without drawing significant loading current from the carbon sheet.

apparatus.name: Point-Contact Copper Tracking Probe
